questions.q: A teacher asked his class whether a camel’s hoofs resemble a horse’s or a buffalo’s, and no one could say. What saying did he then teach them?
options: “Knowledge is found only in books”
Not quite. The article says: “To know that you do not know is half of knowledge”.
“To know that you do not know is half of knowledge”
Yes. That awareness makes one start to notice – the spirit of inquiry.
“Seeing is believing”
Not quite. The article says: “To know that you do not know is half of knowledge”.
“He who asks is a fool for a moment”
Not quite. The article says: “To know that you do not know is half of knowledge”.
questions.rationale: “He quoted an Arabic saying: To know that you do not know is half of knowledge… since all of us did not know that we did not know about a camel’s hoofs, we never paid attention even when camels went past us.”

questions.q: The author says the madrasa gave him his religious base. What did his later study of modern thought add?
options: A wish to live abroad
Not quite. The article says: Objective thinking – forming views by unbiased, logical analysis.
Objective thinking – forming views by unbiased, logical analysis
Right. “An objective thinker is a right thinker.”
Skill in public speaking
Not quite. The article says: Objective thinking – forming views by unbiased, logical analysis.
A dislike of traditional learning
Not quite. The article says: Objective thinking – forming views by unbiased, logical analysis.
questions.rationale: “The greatest thing I acquired from studying modern thought was objective thinking. I had not learned this at the madrasa.”

questions.q: Of what does the gathering of pilgrims on the plain of Arafat remind them?
options: The journey of the caravans
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Reckoning, when all will stand before God.
The markets of old Makkah
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Reckoning, when all will stand before God.
The battles of early history
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Reckoning, when all will stand before God.
The Day of Reckoning, when all will stand before God
Well read. All alike, in simple dress, with one call.
questions.rationale: “The plain of Arafat, where the pilgrims spend one whole day is like a picture of the Day of Reckoning.”

questions.q: Why does the article say that one who does not thank people is unlikely to be grateful to God?
options: A person’s favour is plain to see, while God’s favours are grasped only by reflection – failing at the easier, one fails at the harder
Well reasoned. Ingratitude becomes a habit of mind.
Because God does not need thanks
Not quite. The article says: A person’s favour is plain to see, while God’s favours are grasped only by reflection – failing at the easier, one fails at the harder.
Because people give more than God
Not quite. The article says: A person’s favour is plain to see, while God’s favours are grasped only by reflection – failing at the easier, one fails at the harder.
Because thanking people takes no effort
Not quite. The article says: A person’s favour is plain to see, while God’s favours are grasped only by reflection – failing at the easier, one fails at the harder.
questions.rationale: “One who fails to perceive an event which is directly observable cannot be expected to grasp something which can be apprehended only after a great deal of cogitation.”

questions.q: The lamp flickered while Caliph Umar ibn Abdul Aziz sat with a guest, who offered to wake the servant. What did the Caliph do?
options: Asked the guest to fill it
Not quite. The article says: Got up and filled the lamp himself – he was the same man before and after.
Got up and filled the lamp himself – he was the same man before and after
Yes. Rank does not excuse one from small tasks.
Sat on in the dark
Not quite. The article says: Got up and filled the lamp himself – he was the same man before and after.
Woke the servant himself
Not quite. The article says: Got up and filled the lamp himself – he was the same man before and after.
questions.rationale: “I was Umar ibn Abdul Aziz before I put oil in the lamp, and I am still Umar ibn Adul Aziz.”

questions.q: Abu Hazim was asked how one gives thanks for one’s eyes. What did he answer?
options: By looking only at beautiful things
Not quite. The article says: When you see good, speak of it; when you see evil, pass over it.
By keeping them lowered at all times
Not quite. The article says: When you see good, speak of it; when you see evil, pass over it.
When you see good, speak of it; when you see evil, pass over it
Correct. And likewise with what one hears.
By reading as much as possible
Not quite. The article says: When you see good, speak of it; when you see evil, pass over it.
questions.rationale: “When you behold good, make mention of it and when you behold evil, pass over it.”

questions.article: To Make Up for Our Helplessness
questions.q: Man has no power of his own. What, according to the article, has God given to make up for this?
options: Supplication – one who earnestly asks will be given
Right. His very helplessness, offered in prayer, becomes his means.
A long life in which to try again
Not quite. The article says: Supplication – one who earnestly asks will be given.
Wealth to buy what he needs
Not quite. The article says: Supplication – one who earnestly asks will be given.
Authority over other creatures
Not quite. The article says: Supplication – one who earnestly asks will be given.
questions.rationale: “God has shown us special mercy: He has made supplication sufficient to ensure that we receive.”

questions.q: The article speaks of a “veil” that keeps people from seeing divine signs in nature. What form does it take?
options: Taking everything for granted as mere cause and effect, and looking only for material gain
Yes. So no lesson is drawn.
Living far from the countryside
Not quite. The article says: Taking everything for granted as mere cause and effect, and looking only for material gain.
Poor eyesight in old age
Not quite. The article says: Taking everything for granted as mere cause and effect, and looking only for material gain.
Lack of scientific instruments
Not quite. The article says: Taking everything for granted as mere cause and effect, and looking only for material gain.
questions.rationale: “Satan tries to make man take everything around him for granted and not ponder or reflect upon them.”

questions.q: “The sun cannot overtake the moon… each floats in its own orbit.” What lesson for human society does the article take from this?
options: People should avoid one another
Not quite. The article says: If each person keeps to his own sphere, friction and conflict are avoided.
Society should never change
Not quite. The article says: If each person keeps to his own sphere, friction and conflict are avoided.
If each person keeps to his own sphere, friction and conflict are avoided
Exactly. As the heavenly bodies never collide.
The strong should lead and the weak follow
Not quite. The article says: If each person keeps to his own sphere, friction and conflict are avoided.
questions.rationale: “If man were to apply this principle to his life, everyone would operate in his own given sphere, thus rectifying the friction which exists in human society.”

questions.q: Some asked why the Quran was not revealed to “some great man of the two towns.” What test does the article see in this?
options: To honour the leaders of one’s town
Not quite. The article says: To recognise truth on its own merit, not because a person of rank presents it.
To wait for the majority to decide
Not quite. The article says: To recognise truth on its own merit, not because a person of rank presents it.
To prefer what is new to what is old
Not quite. The article says: To recognise truth on its own merit, not because a person of rank presents it.
To recognise truth on its own merit, not because a person of rank presents it
Well read. Judging by outward grandeur has no value.
questions.rationale: “Acknowledgement of the truth—and here is the greatest test for man—is valid only when the truth recommends itself by virtue of its own merit.”
